record.context_brief: Large product-free sets in nite groups
record.original_question: How large can be a product-free subset of a nite group? A subset A of a group is called product-free if the equation xy = z has no solutions in the elements of A . Babai and S os proved in that any nite group G contains a product-free subset with at least cjGj4=7 elements, where c is a positive absolute constant; Kedlaya improved this to cjGj11=14 in . As shown by Alon and Kleitman , any nite abelian group G contains a product-free subset of size at least 2jGj=7, and this is the best possible bound. In the non-abelian case, already the alternating groups An are of interest; Green conjectures that the largest size of a product-free subset of An is o(jAnj) (as n ! 1). Recently, Gowers has shown that any product-free subset of the group G = PSL2(p) has fewer, than cjGj8=9 elements, for a suitable absolute constant C. (The group PSL2(p), short for projective special linear group, is the quotient group SL2(p)=fI; Ig; here SL2(p) is the multiplicative group of 2 2 matrices over Fp with unit determinant, and I is the 2 2 identity matrix over Fp.)

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A subset $A$ of a group $G$ is called product-free if the equation $xy=z$ has no solutions with $x,y,z\in A$. For each $n\ge 2$, let $A_n$ denote the alternating group on $n$ letters, and let $\mathrm{pf}(A_n)$ denote the maximum size of a product-free subset of $A_n$. Prove or disprove the following conjecture of Green: 
$$\mathrm{pf}(A_n)=o(|A_n|)\quad\text{as }n\to\infty,$$
i.e., for every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $N$ such that for all $n\ge N$, every product-free subset $A\subseteq A_n$ satisfies $|A|<\varepsilon\,|A_n|$. More quantitatively, determine the correct order of magnitude of $\mathrm{pf}(A_n)/|A_n|$.
artifact.status_search_result: Green's conjecture that the largest product-free subset of $A_n$ has density $o(1)$ was established by Gowers (via his theory of quasirandom groups), giving density at most $n^{-1/3}$. Eberhard improved this to $O(n^{-1/2}\log^{7/2}n)$, and a 2022/2024 work of Keevash, Lifshitz and Minzer determined the maximum density up to constants as $\Theta(n^{-1/2})$, settling the qualitative conjecture and pinning down the order of magnitude.

status_evidence.title: On the largest product-free subsets of the alternating groups
status_evidence.snippet: In 1985 Babai and Sós conjectured that A_n contains a product-free set of constant density. This was refuted by Gowers; Eberhard improved the bound; the largest product-free subset of A_n has density Θ(n^{-1/2}).
status_evidence.claim: Green's conjecture (density o(1)) is solved, with the sharp order Θ(n^{-1/2}).

status_evidence.title: On the largest product-free subsets of the alternating groups (arXiv)
status_evidence.snippet: Gowers showed product-free subsets of A_n have density at most n^{-1/3}; Eberhard improved this to O(n^{-1/2} log^{7/2} n); we determine the maximum density up to constants.
status_evidence.claim: The conjecture is proved and the optimal density is determined.
